summary: For children aged 5–7, teach the five senses as a sense–organ–stimulus triple: eyes detect light, ears detect sound, skin detects pressure and temperature, tongue detects flavours, nose detects smells. Lead with direct experience at hands-on stations, then have children name the sense, the body part, and what it picked up. Beyond naming, build the idea that each sense detects a different KIND of information and that senses often work together (especially taste and smell for flavour). Keep it everyday and age-appropriate — no eye/ear anatomy or wave physics yet. This also lays groundwork for the idea that all senses report to the brain.
misconceptions: 'We have exactly five senses and that's all' — fine as an age-appropriate model, but balance and body-position senses exist too (keep as a light aside).
'Taste comes only from the tongue' — missing that smell contributes much of flavour.
'Skin only feels touch' — missing that it also detects temperature and pain.
'You hear/see with your brain-eyes' — confusing the organ that detects with the brain that interprets; the organ detects, the brain makes sense of it.
'The tongue has zones for each taste' — the old 'tongue map' myth; tastes are detected all over the tongue.
'Senses work separately' — not seeing that they combine to build one picture of the world.

activities.title: Sense stations: use it, then name it
steps: Visit hands-on stations and USE each sense before naming it: a feely bag (reach in and feel without looking), sound jars or a listening game, smell pots, a taste tray, and spot-it pictures.
After each station, say three things aloud: the sense used, the body part (organ) that detected it, and WHAT it picked up — e.g. 'touch, my skin, it felt bumpy and cold'.
Match five cards that pair each sense to its organ and to an everyday example: eyes catch a rainbow, ears catch a barking dog, skin feels warm sand, tongue tastes lemon, nose smells baking.
activities.insight: Each sense uses a particular body part to detect a different kind of information about the world.

activities.title: Senses team up: the nose-hold taste test
steps: Before tasting, predict: 'If I pinch my nose shut, will I still tell these two flavours apart?' Say why you think so.
Taste two foods with the same texture but different flavours (e.g. two jellybean flavours, or finely grated apple and pear) with the nose pinched, then again with the nose open, and compare.
Say what changed and which two senses were working together.
activities.insight: Taste and smell cooperate: much of flavour comes from smell, so for flavour the tongue does not do the job by itself — these two senses combine to build the taste you recognise. (This is about flavour specifically; other senses can still work on their own.)

activities.title: Tongue-map myth buster
steps: Taste a strong flavour (e.g. something sour or salty) touched to different parts of the tongue, such as the tip and each side.
Notice whether you can taste the same flavour in each place you tried, not just in one 'zone'.
State the myth and the correction in your own words: 'There are no separate zones for each taste.'
activities.insight: The old 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth: taste buds on the tip, sides and back of the tongue can each pick up all the basic tastes. The middle has fewer taste buds, so tastes can feel weaker there.

activities.title: Which sense would help? Reasoning game
steps: Blindfolded, hold a slice of orange and work out which senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what each one would be picking up.
Explain why your EYES can't help right now (they need light and are covered).
Try a drag-and-match: move stimuli (a bell, a flower, an ice cube) to the sense that detects each, and answer 'how do you know it's raining without looking?'
activities.insight: Different senses detect different information, so you can pick the right sense for a situation and explain when one (like sight) can't help.

checkQuestion: You're blindfolded and someone hands you a slice of orange. Which of your senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what would each one be picking up? And why can't your EYES help you right now?
checkAnswer: With eyes blindfolded, sight can't help because it needs light and your eyes are covered. But smell (nose picking up the orange's odour), taste (tongue detecting its flavour), and touch (skin and fingers feeling the bumpy peel and wetness) can still identify it — each sense detects a different kind of information. Hearing wouldn't help much here. Each sense uses a different body part to detect a different thing.
